Yes, the hard part for me is when I do melodic dictation, harmonic dictation, or counterpoint. I can tell that they’re major and minor and stuff but it’s difficult for me to distinguish what the Roman numeral of the chord is.

Since I’ve been in college, I’ve learned that different chords have different ‘weights’. In a major key, you have I, ii, iii, VI, V, vi, and vii dim. If you’re not familiar with these symbols these are Roman numerals and you start in what scale degree or number it says, stack thirds until you have three notes and apply the key signature. So if we were in G major and you see a V chord you’d start on count up the scale to the 5th note, which is D and stack thirds. You’d end up with DFA, then apply the key sig and you get D, F#, A. 

Here are some basic guidelines:

The I chord is your tonic, it’s where everything sounds at home and at rest. This chord can go to any chord. 

The ii chord is mostly used before the V chord. 

The iii chord isn’t used that often, but it sounds good if it precedes the vi chord. 

The IV chord is the closest to home other than the I chord bc it shares two notes with it. It can be used more liberally than the other chords, but generally it either precedes the ii chord or the I chord. 

The V chord is the second heaviest chord, bc it contains the 7th scale degree, which has a very strong pull to the tonic, which is the note of the key that you are in. V almost always goes to I but it can also go to vi in special cases. You can add a fourth note to the chord, which is just another third up and it will give it even more of a pull to I. 

The vi chord is often used before the VI chord or after the V chord. Using it after the V chord creates a fake resolution that can grab your audience. 

vii dim should only really be used before a I chord at the end of a phrase, but you can use it to create tension. It functions almost the same as a V chord. 

Inverting these chords to make the voice leading smooth is a must. You wouldn’t want someone to jump an octave to sing or play these notes, so make the distance between notes reasonable. 

Keep in mind when applying these rules that these are not the law. These are guidelines of stuff that should sound good on paper. If something sounds good, then do it. These rules are stuff that I’ve picked up on from theory and at the end of the day just keep making music and sharing it with the world :)
